newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Divers hunt for gun that killed Sweden PM Palme.
newsitem.headline: Divers hunt for gun that killed Sweden PM Palme.

text.p: The unsolved 1986 murder of Swedish Prime Minister Olof Palme was back in the spotlight on Tuesday as a team of divers began a search of central Stockholm waters for the gun that killed him.
A Swedish-Norwegian team will search the five-metre (16.5-foot) deep floor of the Klara Sjo (Lake Klara) where the murder weapon may have been thrown, police said.
The project, codenamed Operation .357 after the calibre of gun used kill Palme, will concentrate on Klara Sjo following a deathbed confession of an Stockholm underworld figure in 1993.
"The police are not taking part in the search itself but if a murder weapon is found we will investigate it," Lars Nylen, head of the National Investigation Department, told Swedish news agency TT.
Two Norwegian companies are financing the project, which will involve state-of-the-art ultrasound techniques and is estimated to cost between 500,000 and one million crowns ($124,000).

Police have never found the Smith & Wesson .357 Magnum revolver which was used to kill Palme with a single bullet as he returned home from the cinema with his wife on February 28, 1986. This has been a stumbling block to solving the murder.

Donald Forsberg, a Swedish diver leading Operation .357, told the tabloid newspaper Aftonbladet that there were several reasons behind his efforts, including a 50-million-crown reward for solving the murder.
A decision by Swedish police earlier this year not to dive to try to find for the weapon was also a factor, he said.
"Money is always important of course and this is something to strive for. But we are adventurers. Carrying out projects like this is a way of life," Forsberg told Aftonbladet.
Seven Norwegian divers were using two weeks of their holiday to help with the project.

Norwegian Anton Smith said he wanted to test his company's system that can use sound waves to penetrate layers of silt, estimated to be several metres (yards) thick, on the sea floor and detect metal objects.
"My main aims are two-fold -- to prove this technology works and to possibly solve the murder of Palme once and for all," Smith said.

The search was concentrated on the Klara Sjo because of the testimony of Lars Tingstrom, known as the Bomb Man, who disclosed in a 1993 deathbed confession that he was part of a gang of four involved in the murder.

His lawyer, Pelle Svensson, said Tingstrom's confession stated that the gang also included Christer Pettersson, who was convicted of Palme's murder in 1988 but later acquitted, as well as a former bank robber and an explosives expert, now dead. ($ = 8.049 Swedish Crowns)
